corrections.was: The same twenty-five check test, timed two ways. Real time, twenty-two point four seconds. With the fixed f p s flag at sixty, zero point three four seconds, about sixty-six times faster, with identical results. A fixed frame rate locks a run to a set number of frames a second. A pinned time step forces every simulation step to one length. For example, the agent runs your platformer's test at a fixed frame rate, so each step is the same length on any machine.
corrections.now: The same twenty-five check test, timed two ways. Real time, twenty-two point four seconds. With the fixed f p s flag at sixty, zero point three four seconds, about sixty-six times faster, with identical results. A fixed frame rate makes every frame count as the same amount of game time, without waiting for the wall clock. A pinned time step forces every simulation step to one length. For example, the agent runs your platformer's test at a fixed frame rate, so each step is the same length on any machine.
corrections.why: 'Locks a run to a set number of frames a second' implies wall-clock frames (yet the run went about 66 times faster than real time) and echoes the slide's 'rendering' wording; Chapter 0 says --fixed-fps makes each frame exactly 1/fps of game time and disables real-time sync, and nothing is drawn headless (Chapter 1: steps without waiting for the wall clock).

corrections.was: Second, was it headless, with the time step pinned? A run in a window, or with real-time steps, may not repeat the same way twice.
corrections.now: Second, was it headless, with the time step pinned? A run with real-time steps may not repeat the same way twice.
corrections.why: Nothing in the references says running in a window makes a run unrepeatable; Chapter 0 puts the cause on real-time steps (no --fixed-fps), so the window clause states a false cause.
